"Very well. When you are confident that your fortress can withstand anything the Aztecs can throw at it, return here. Then we will rally the army and march on Tenochtitlan."
Fortify
Return to your fortress and prepare your people to defend against an attack by the Aztec Empire.
Continue.

"It has been some time since you last received a reward that has done your invaluable service justice. Our coffers are of course stretched to their limits due to the impending war, but my servants will bring a chest to your caravan full of jewellery, statuettes, and other gold and silver trinkets."
"You are very generous."
The chieftain smiles.
"Good luck with your fortress. We will await your return."
"About time."
The chieftain scoffs.
"Yes, well. Go see to your fortress. We will await your return."

A little coldly, the palace staff informs you that Tepictoton is in some important meeting or another concerning the impending attack on Tenochtitlan. You are also apparently no longer invited to stay in the palace while you are in the city, though you will be tolerated to set up camp just outside the city limits.

With many regrets, the palace staff informs you that Tepictoton is in some important meeting or another concerning the impending attack on Tenochtitlan. As a trusted ally of the Totonac, you are invited to stay in the palace and make use of any of the modest luxuries its staff has on offer.
Tepictoton is neck deep in strategic, logistic, and diplomatic meetings. Despite this, he has your servants immediately show you in when you return.
"PName! I was wondering when you might return, but the reconstruction of a stronghold is not carried out overnight, I realise this. How is the work progressing?"
"It is finished, the fortress has been restored."
Rebuild Fortaleza Gutiérrez
"PName! Back so soon? Is the fortress rebuilt?"
"Not yet."
He doesn't even look annoyed that you disturbed him. In fact he looks like he's altogether /too busy/ to have time for annoyance.
"Right right, well do come back when you're ready, our own preparations are going well, but we can't start the war until we know our western flank is secure!"
You are escorted to Tepictoton by an uncommonly large group of guards. In his throne room, he is flanked by even more guards. He may no longer trust you entirely.
"Have you collected the 5000 Valuables to be paid in restitution for the massacre of Papantla?"
"I have. My servants are bringing them to the palace as we speak."
Restitution
The chieftain takes a moment to collect himself, then somehow manages to proceed as though nothing had happened.
"Where were we?"
"I have not."
The look he gives you is absolutely withering.
"Then. I would suggest. You do so."

Tepictoton has recently returned from Papantla when you return from your business at the Aztec farms. The chieftain looks quite distraught - he's pacing in circles around his stool with such heavy steps as to make you worry for the health of the floor.
"Those bastards! Those cowards! Those honourless /murderers!/"
"What's happened?"
He turns to you and stops. His voice is shaking.

"Papantla has been destroyed! The city is burned to the ground, not a single living witness remains! I'm telling you PName, you can't begin to imagine the sight that met us when we arrived. The sheer... carnage!"
"I don't know what to say."
He shakes his head.
"It's only a matter of time before Moctezuma attempts to subject us to the same fate. We must fortify our position, and then it is time to strike at the Aztecs."
"No need to imagine. I destroyed Papantla."

Tepictoton has recently returned from Papantla when you return from your business at the Aztec farms. The chieftain sits in his own dark thoughts as you enter, resting his head heavily on his hand. He looks up at you with the deepest of frowns.
"Papantla has been attacked. By /white men!/"
"That's impossible."
He stands suddenly, with his shoulders drawn all the way up to his ears.
"IS IT?! Tell me you had no hand in this, PName!"
[Check Diplomacy Medium] "It must have been remnants of Gutiérrez's group."
Tepictoton regards you skeptically.
"That seems unlikely."
Tepictoton kicks his stool, which flies half-way across the floor, making a considerably ruckus.
"A LIE! A BAREFACED LIE! It was /you/! The witnesses describe /your/ people! Explain yourself!"
"I can't. I attacked Papantla."
Tepictoton's face grows quite red.
"YOU VILE BANDIT! How dare you fall in our backs like this?! What possible boon do you stand to gain from such a strike against our allies?!"
[Check Diplomacy Easy] "Their chieftain, Xīlōxōch, had plans to murder me and my people. I won't guess at her motivations, but she must have seen me as a threat."
Tepictoton regards you skeptically.
"So it was self-defence?"
Continue.
Anacaona doesn't say a word. She stands in the back, wringing her hands.
"I assure you I had no hand in it."
He looks at you in silence for a long time, then he shakes his head slightly.

"Fine. This is a bad thing for us both, and I believe you. With the warriors of Papantla slaughtered, it's only a matter of time before Moctezuma attempts to subject us to the same fate. We must fortify our position, and then it is time to strike at the Aztecs."
He stares at you for a long moment, and it's pretty clear he knows you're lying.
"I cannot possibly believe you. What you have done... is despicable. I want you to understand that. You and your men are responsible for the deaths of thousands of innocent women and children."
Continue.
"I make no excuses for my actions."
"The situation got out of control."

Tepictoton doesn't seem to know if he should laugh, cry, or attempt to run you through with his spear. It takes him a few minutes to get his inner turmoil under control, and then he folds his face into a determined, pragmatic expression.

"You must pay restitution for the victims of Papantla. We, the Totonac, need you in this upcoming war, but our alliance is off to a poor start indeed! You must pay restitution on the order of 5000 Valuables for what you have done. Only then can we proceed."
"I accept that. My servants will bring 5000 Valuables to your palace."
The chieftain sits down, looking shaken. He takes a moment to collect himself, then somehow manages to proceed as though nothing had happened.
"Where were we?"
"I will not pay that."
The old chieftain screams so loudly you're sure his words are heard at the other end of the city, and spittle flies from his lips.
"I WILL HAVE NOTHING TO DO WITH YOU UNTIL YOU WILL PAY THE RESTITUTION, NOR WILL ANYBODY IN THIS CITY!"
"I cannot afford that."
The old chieftain shakes his head angrily.

"Then you must acquire the sum and bring it to me when you have it! Nobody in this city will have any dealings with you until the price has been paid! If any of our allies were to find out about the massacre, they would turn on us and flay us both alive. And that's to say nothing of my personal... /repulsion/ of your actions!"
Raze The Farms
Restitution
Bring 5000 Valuables to Tepictoton in Xalapa if you wish to proceed with your plans to make war on the Aztecs.
Continue.
Tepictoton calls in his guards to show you out, looking somewhat shaken as he sinks back onto his stool.
Tepictoton has recently returned from Papantla when you return from your business at the Aztec farms. He looks tired, but pleased to see you again.
"I hope your business went as well as mine, PName. It took some effort, but Papantla is with us."
"Those farms will not be supplying Tenochtitlan any longer."
Raze The Farms
"Then our chances against the Aztecs are significantly improved, but you'll excuse me if I offer you no reward this time, in light of... your recent actions."
"Then our chances against the Aztecs are significantly improved, and your reward will be delivered forthwith."
Continue.
"I have one more opportunity to bring to your attention. To the west is a stronghold build by your predecessor, after he passed through Xalapa."
Continue.
"It has been abandoned for a long time. If you were to hold this stronghold, we would be well defended against an Aztec attack from the west."
"I have already been to that fortress."
"I will find that stronghold and look into the matter."
Rebuild Fortaleza Gutiérrez
Rebuild the Spanish fortress west of Xalapa and return to Tepictoton when the reconstruction is complete.
Tepictoton once again insistingly shakes your hand.
"Reclaim it and restore it to its former glory. When you return, the Totonac peoples will be ready to go to war. Good luck - to all of us!"

"It has come to my attention that you have reclaimed and rebuilt your predecessor's fortress in the west. No love was lost between my people and his, but I must respect the masonry of your people! Not as imposing as the pyramids of our cities, but it cannot be faulted on practical application!"
"It needed a little work, but it's in good shape again."
"Then our western flank is secure. Now is the time to strike the first direct blow against an Aztec settlement!"
"I propose we attack Cuautitlán before we attempt to take Tenochtitlan itself."
The chieftain nods.
"Perfect. Precisely what I had in mind."
Continue.
Tepictoton clears his throat.
"My plan is for you to attack Cuautitlán first."
Continue.
Raze Cuautitlán
Travel to the Aztec settlement of Cuautitlán and raze it in preparation for a full-scale assault on Tenochtitlan. Tepictoton has sent a contingent of his warriors there to help you.
"Their warriors pose a minor threat, but as long as the Aztecs control that territory, they can use it against us. We must hold every acre of land north of Tenochtitlan if we hope to stand a chance."
Continue.
"Though Cuautitlán is ravaged by disease, it is a sizeable settlement and I do not expect you to conquer it alone. I have sent a contingent of my warriors ahead to Cuautitlán to aid you."
"I will obliterate Cuautitlán from the surface of this land."
"I am loathe to attack innocents, but if Cuautitlán must fall, I will see to it."
"I will pay a visit to Cuautitlán."
This time, you notice, Tepictoton does not shake your hand.
Tepictoton shakes your hand.
"Moctezuma will not take kindly to a direct attack on his empire so close to Tenochtitlan. Prepare yourself for war, PName. Once Cuautitlán falls, there is no going back. For any of us."
You are informed that Tepictoton is out of town again on diplomatic business. As an ally of the Totonac, you are invited to make yourself at home in the chieftain's personal quarters while he's out.
Tepictoton has returned from his diplomatic tour of the Totonac tribes. He welcomes you back to Xalapa with a smile on his face so big it reaches all the way from his left ear to his right.

"Do I have some great news for /you/, PName! Although there was a small disagreement with Cempoala, all the Totonac chiefs have agreed to join me against Tenochtitlan! With the combined might of our tribes, and the military aid of Tlaxcala, we now pose the most significant threat to their power that the Aztecs have ever faced!"
"Did you talk to Cihuātōn? We were attacked by warriors from Cempoala."
Tepictoton's grin fades.
"That conniving old bastard. Did you deal with it?"
"We killed the attackers and kept the envoys alive. The meeting concluded quickly after that, and it seems Tlaxcala are on board."
Protect The Envoy
"Thank the gods you were there to help and protect Cihuātōn. I will have your reward brought to your servants as soon as our business here is concluded."
"We were attacked by warriors from Cempoala! The envoys were killed."
Protect The Envoy
Tepictoton's grin freezes, and he stares at you in a faintly maniacal way for a moment. Then he shrugs and sits back down on his stool.

"That's... very bad news. I'm glad you made it out alive, but this means we've lost the support of Tlaxcala. They will know the Totonac were to blame for that attack. How could they follow us into battle after that?"
"Why would Cempoala sabotage us?"

"The chieftain of Cempoala considers his city the capital of the Totonac people, and he was not open to yielding any of his power. He was nothing but trouble when I came to that city, but thanks to the idol I was able to exert my influence behind the scenes and, long story short, he was overruled by his elders and Cempoala has joined our cause without him."
Continue.
"He must have caught wind of my plans to negotiate with Tlaxcala and sent his warriors to ruin the meeting before I visited the city. Perhaps he thought that was the sticking point of my plans."
"Perhaps it's time we move directly against the Aztec."
Tepictoton stands up and starts pacing around the room.

"Not quite yet, my friend. We need time to rally the Totonac armies - there is equipment to be constructed, supply lines to be established, battle plans to be... planned. We can't strike directly against an Aztec settlement until we're ready for war."
"I'm not going to just sit on my hands. Is there any way to weaken them without setting off the war?"
He places a hand on your shoulder.

"You're right. How about this: You can hit their supply lines. If you attack and raze their farms, they will not be able to withstand a prolonged siege, yet it will not be enough to provoke a full-scale response from them."
"What now?"

"We can't strike directly against an Aztec settlement until we're ready for war. In the meantime, you can strike a blow against the enemy by hitting their supply lines. If you attack and raze their farms, they will not be able to withstand a prolonged siege, yet it will not be enough to provoke a full-scale response from them."
"You want me to kill defenceless peasants?"
He throws up his hands.

"These people are far from innocent! That land used to be ours, home to the Totonac people. When the Aztec wanted to expand their influence, they rolled in and took that land by force to use for agriculture. Since then, they've been exploiting it to the very limit of its capacity."
"I'll pay them a visit."
"Sounds easy enough, I'll take care of it."
He raises his hand in warning.
"Don't underestimate them. They may just be peasants, but they took that land from the Totonac by force, and they will not give it up without a fight."
"I'll take the necessary precautions."
"Killing peasants? I'll consider it recreation for my troops."
He suddenly looks a little uncomfortable.
"Right, well. It would improve our position when we hit Tenochtitlan, in any case."
Continue.
Raze The Farms
Attack and raze the Aztec farms north of Tenochtitlan.
Tepictoton again shakes your hand firmly.
"Good luck, PName. I will take care of the logistics for the war in the meantime. Return here when you have dealt with the farms."
It seems Tepictoton hasn't returned from his diplomatic journey yet. His people are very apologetic, but they're forced to ask you to return again tomorrow and see if he's back.

You are informed that Tepictoton has left for his diplomatic journey. As a friend of the city, you are given more or less free reign of his palace while he's away - only his personal quarters are off-limits.
Let the enormous jaguar loose in the city.
Attack Xalapa.
Leave.

A group of warriors intercept you on the way into the city and demand to take you to Tepictoton immediately. The chief jumps off his stool as you enter his throne room, pointing an angry finger at you.
"You have some gall returning here after what you did!"
"Anacaona was not abducted, she /wanted/ to join us."
He waves his hand angrily in front of his face.

"I know that! But you /killed/ 12 of our warriors! Twelve brave men and women who were only serving their chieftain! If my daughter wants to run off on some dangerous adventure that's between me and her, but did you really have to kill everybody who tried to stop you?!"
"When I am attacked, I defend myself."
He rolls his eyes.

"Yes, well... I suppose there is reason in that. Let's forget this entire misadventure ever happened. And seeing how she apparently feels so strongly about it, my daughter can remain under your command - as long as you promise to look after her."
"I promise."
Continue.
"My sincere apologies. It got out of hand."
The chieftain snorts.

"That would have to be /some/ apology to make up for so many senseless deaths! However, in the interest of maintaining good relations with you and your people in the long term, I will forget that this whole misadventure ever happened."
Continue.
Tepictoton receives you in his throne room without making a fuss.
"I was wondering if you'd have the guts to come back here after you made off with my daughter!"
"She insisted on joining us."
He waves his hand dismissively.
"I'm certain she did, seeing how she won't shut up about going on an adventure and seeing the world. If she doesn't want to get married yet, so be it - she hardly had to go and get herself abducted."
Continue.
The chieftain leans forward and levels his daughter with a stern gaze.
"You and I will have to have a talk in private after my business with PName is concluded, daughter. We must discuss the topic of /parental authority/."
Continue.
Anacaona squirms.
"I have brought you the idol."
The chieftain leans forward and runs his gaze across your expedition members.
"Where /is/ my daughter? I think I'd like to talk to her in private, concering the topic of parental authority."
"She's... back at the caravan."
"She's... back at the caravan."
"Tell your servants to bring her here so she can make up with her worried father and get a /proper/ send-off."
"That will have to wait. I have brought you the idol."
"She's at our caravan, recovering from a minor mishap."
"What /kind/ of mishap? No, wait, don't tell me. I don't want to know. This sort of thing comes with a more active life-style, I suppose, I have to learn to trust her to take care of herself."
"I have brought you the idol."
Tepictoton receives you in his throne room, eager with anticipation. Anacaona is back at his side, watching miserably as your expedition members file into the room.
"I have brought you the idol."
Tepictoton's Idol
Tepictoton accepts the idol with something approaching reverence.

"/Amazing/. Last time I saw this idol was years ago, but I remember it like it was yesterday. My father was a fool to give this away - he never even realised the political power it unlocks. With this in my hands, all the other chieftains will fall right in line behind me as I march upon Tenochtitlan."
"I believe I am due some manner of reward."
The chieftain chuckles.
"I suspected you would bring that up! Of course, I will have baskets of gold and jade brought to your servants."
"I hope it's that easy."
The chieftain laughs.
"It will be nothing of the sort! But I will make it happen, thanks to you. And I believe you were promised a reward. I will have baskets of gold and jade brought to your servants."
Continue.
"While I secure the loyalty of the Totonac tribes, we must meet with the Tlaxcalteca. Again, we need your help. Have you had dealings with Tlaxcala before?"
"I have not."
He scoots to the edge of his stool. It creaks ominously.

"Tlaxcala is a nation that exists independently within the borders of the Aztec Empire. Can you imagine how much that must annoy the Aztec? I can certainly imagine it, and the very thought of it warms my heart."
"Do you consider Tlaxcala to be your allies?"
"I have."

"We have an uneasy relationship with Tlaxcala, but they are fearsome warriors and we could use them on our side in the battle against the Aztec. So, as you might expect, I've arranged a diplomatic meeting with envoys of Tlaxcala."
Continue.

"I was hoping to meet Tlaxcala on neutral ground, but we are running out of time and I had to acquiesce to their demands - we are meeting underground in a Tlaxcalan tomb. I don't quite trust them, you understand, so I want somebody to watch over the meeting and make sure they don't try anything."
"So /this/ is where we come in."
Tepictoton grins conspiratorially.

"I can't very well send a group of my own warriors, the Tlaxcalteca would never attend under those circumstances. You will be perceived as neutral, as they don't realise that you're working with us. Simply attend the negotiations and keep an eye out for trouble."
"I will go to the meeting and make sure nothing happens."
"If the Tlaxcalteca so much as looks at your envoy the wrong way, we will kill them."
"I'll watch over the proceedings."
Protect The Envoy
Bring Cihuātōn to the Tlaxcalan tomb and watch over her diplomatic meeting with the envoy from Tlaxcala.

"I shall immediately travel to Papantla and Cempoala with the idol and begin negotiations with their chieftains. I have appointed our elder Cihuātōn to meet with Tlaxcala, and I have been informed that they are sending a man by the name of Ēlōxōchitl."
"Understood."
The chieftain shakes your hand firmly.
"Let's hope everything goes according to plan. Good luck."

Chief Tepictoton will not see you, and his guards politely but firmly turn you away at the door. Everything generally seems a little tense right now, after the business with Anacaona's "abduction" and such.
Chief Tepictoton will not see you, and his guards politely but firmly turn you away at the door.
Demand to see Tepictoton.

You make it clear that your business is extremely urgent and the consequences for denying your audience would be severe. Eventually the guards cave and - annoyed - take you to see Tepictoton. The chieftain is surprised to see you again when you've nothing to report, but he lends you his ear nevertheless.
"We need to talk about your relationship with Tenochtitlan."
He looks confused.
"What 'relationship'? There is no relationship, only tension that is about to turn into open hostilities, if everything goes according to plan!"
"Everything has not gone according to plan. You relied too much on my help."
"Emperor Moctezuma would very much like you to give up your rebellion."
Tepictoton's face turns pale.
"No! /You/ have allied yourself with Tenochtitlan?"
"Tenochtitlan demands your unconditional surrender."
Tepictoton's face turns pale.
"What did you just say?!"
"Surrender, or you will face terrible consequences."
The chieftain strikes a rather imposing posture and points at you threateningly.

"I will /never/ surrender! You think your puny group will make any real difference in the end?! When I march on Tenochtitlan with thousands of warriors, and the Aztec meets my army with their own, what more will a dozen Spaniards mean?"
"Anacaona, come here a moment."
"Don't underestimate me, chieftain."
He laughs angrily.
"Anacaona, come here a moment."
Anacaona steps forward and stands next to you. The chieftain jumps up off his stool.
"She's injured! What have you done?!"
Anacaona steps forward and stands next to you. The chieftain stands up with a deep frown.
"I can tell that your daughter means a lot to you."
He simply nods.
"It would be tragic if something were to /happen/ to her."
Tepictoton bites his lip so hard it bleeds.
"What is the meaning of this?"
Draw your knife and put your arm around her.
Anacaona squirms a little bit under your touch. Tepictoton takes a quick step forward, but stops himself.
"Don't..."
"People sometimes forget how hard war can be for the women and the children. Their sufferings are forgotten in the search for glory."
"I want to reach a peaceful solution to this conflict. A solution where nobody gets... /hurt/."
You can see the chieftain's heart sink.
"Please. Let my daughter go. Give her back to me, and I will end the hostilities."
"Do you swear it on your honour?"
Tepictoton is looking more destroyed by the second.
"On my honour."
Let Anacaona go.

You release Anacaona and Tepictoton rushes over to grab her and pull her away from you. The girl herself is looking a little confused. He hurriedly exchanges a few words with her in their own language, and then he gives her to two of the champions who take her away to another part of the building.
Continue.

In exchange for the safe return of his daughter, Tepictoton has sworn to keep Xalapa out of the Totonac attack on Tenochtitlan, though he can't stop the attack altogether. Return to Moctezuma to report the outcome of your mission.
Tepictoton straightens up and brushes off his clothes.
"All right, PName. I yield. For the safety of my daughter, I will seize my involvement with the Totonac rebellion, and I will send no warriors of Xalapa to Tenochtitlan when the attack takes place."
"That's not good enough, you have to stop the attack!"
He shakes his head heavily.

"Such a thing will not be possible. I have set things into motion that are far too great for you or I to control. Even without Papantla and Xalapa, the Totonac tribes number in the hundreds, and Cempoala will doubtlessly rally their warriors and lead them against Tenochtitlan."
"There must be something you can do to prevent the war!"

Your people scramble to draw their weapons and withdraw from the palace. Your forces are routed out into the plaza in front of the palace, where you manage to regroup with the Aztec division that Quappiatl has sent to face Tepictoton's elite. During the chaos, Anacaona seems to have disappeared.

Your people scramble to draw their weapons and withdraw from the palace. Your forces are routed out into the plaza in front of the palace, where you manage to regroup with the Aztec division that Quappiatl has sent to face Tepictoton's elite.

Deciding that a distraction would be a great way to start your attack on Xalapa, you have the giant jaguar brought to the outskirts of the city, and then you open its cage. And run like hell away from the city.

As you'd hoped, the jaguar ignores you and heads straight for the much more target-rich environment that is the city centre. Judging from the screams, the crying, and the blood-curdling growls, you seem to have executed one hell of a distraction indeed.

With a large part of Xalapa's defences in utter disarray, desperately attempting to contain the jaguar's rampage, and another part off with Tepictoton on his diplomatic errand, this is perhaps the best possible time you could have chosen to attack the city.

As you roll into the city centre with a large division of Aztec warriors behind you, you catch a glimpse of a large group of warriors chasing into the jungle after the jaguar. The remaining defenders of the city scramble to counter this new unexpected threat.

With a large part of Xalapa's defences in utter disarray, desperately attempting to contain the jaguar's rampage, Tepictoton is left with just his personal guard to counter your surprise attack. With a large division of Aztec warriors behind you, your forces meet Tepictoton's in the centre of the city.

Taking advantage of Tepictoton's absense, you decide to attack Xalapa now, while the Totonac city is without its regular leadership. You rendezvous with a large division of Aztec warriors sent by Quappiatl to aid you, and then you roll into the city.

Your part of the fight finishes a bit before the city is taken, and your troops disperse to help the Aztecs mop up the last pockets of resistance. When the city is secure, the Aztecs re-assemble in the market and cheer for you and your troops, as well as each other.

Even though Tepictoton wasn't here, you've struck a great blow against the Totonac uprising by removing Xalapa's warriors from the equation.

Surprisingly, Anacaona emerges again after the battle, and is almost skewered by an Aztec warrior before you order him to stay his hand and let her through. She stares at her feet and speaks even faster than usual.
"I'm sorry I fled but I couldn't bear to fight my father's people I've known most of them my entire life."
"You still wish to follow me after what I've done?"
"My father is gone and I don't know where he is and now the city is under Aztec control I'm not safe here any longer and I don't have any other place to go."

Her voice is faint.

Tears well up in her eyes, and she's visibly fighting to suppress them.

African Slaves of Hispaniola

The first African slaves landed on Hispaniola in 1501, and were destined for the mines. Spain was building an Empire and needed the riches of the new world; its gold and silver and the crops of sugarcanes.

In the early days of the Spanish conquest, the local Indians were used as free labour. Later they were enslaved and forced to work by the Spanish. But the Indian population decreased rapidly, partly because of the wars, but also due to diseases brought by the Europeans, such as measles and the flu. In 1500, it is estimated that there were about 50 million Indians in the Americas. By 1600, this number had been reduced to about 8 million.

The Spanish authorities were alarmed at this decline in the local Indian population. New laws made by the Spanish in 1542 put an end to them being taken as slaves. Instead, a new system (the encomienda) was introduced according to which the Indians were obliged to do a certain amount of work for the Spanish landowner on whose land they lived, they were now serfs instead of slaves - though the difference was negligible.

To keep up the output of the mines or the plantations, the number of imported African slaves was increased. At first they were brought from other colonies owned by Spain, such as the Canary Islands in the Atlantic Ocean. Later, slaves were brought in greater numbers from West Africa.

The licence to sell slaves went to whomever was prepared to pay the most for it. Often this meant that Portuguese, Dutch, German, British, or Genoese merchants were supplying slaves to the Spanish colonies. From 1550 to 1595, the official records show that 36,300 enslaved Africans were imported into the Spanish-owned parts of South America. The number was probably much higher, as more were smuggled in by unlicensed slave traders.

In 1574, a census taken of the Greater Antilles reported 1000 Spaniards and 12,000 African slaves on Hispaniola.
Alcazar de Colon

The Alcazar de Colon was built in the period 1510 - 1512 using the slave labour of 1500 natives. It was built with coral rock in a mixture of the Mudejar and Gothic styles (without use of any nails). The palace consisted of about 50 rooms and was the residence of Diego Colon, son of Christopher Columbus, when he was the Viceroy of Española and the Indies.

The Alcazar de Colon played a strategic role in the Spanish conquest and colonisation of America. It was here Cortez, Pizarro, Balboa, and Velasquez planned their conquests of Mexico, Peru, Panama, and Cuba.
Aztec Empire

The Aztec Empire is the best documented of all the American civilizations at that time. Extensive records have been left by soldiers, friars, scholars, and historians, describing all aspects of Aztec life.

At the time of the Spanish conquest, the Aztecs dominated the northern Mexico. The Aztecs called themselves Mexicas or Tenocha. After a long period of wandering, the tribes that made up the Aztecs settled in the central basin of Mexico. In 1325 they founded the town Tenochtitlan where Mexico City lies today.

During the 15th century, they created an empire that was second only to the empire of the Incas. Their empire was highly organized with a central administration, a diverse and highly specialised society, an extensive trading network, and an agricultural economy adjusted to the land.

At the time of the Spanish conquest in the early 16th century, the Aztec empire under Emperor Montezuma was the most powerful Mesoamerican kingdom of all time. Its population was 15 million people, living in 38 provinces. It covered more than 80,000 square miles and stretched from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf Coast and from central Mexico to the present-day Guatamala.
Caribs

About 100 years prior to the Spanish invasion, the Taínos were challenged by an invading South American tribe - the Caribs. Fierce, warlike, and adept at using poison-tipped arrows, they raided Taíno settlements for slaves - especially female slaves - and took Taíno bodies for their rites of cannibalism. It has been argued that the preeminence of the Taínos, shaken by the attacks of the Caribs, was already jeopardized by the time of the Spanish occupation.

In fact, it was Caribs who fought the most effectively against the Europeans. Their behaviour probably led the Europeans to unfairly attribute warlike tendencies to all of the island's tribes. A dynamic tension between the Taínos and the Caribs certainly existed when Christopher Columbus landed on Hispaniola.
Catedral de Santa María la Menor

Catedral de Santa María la Menor, aka. Cathedral of St. Mary of the Incarnation in Santo Domingo, is the oldest cathedral in the Americas. Consecrated by Pope Julius II in 1504, the construction of the Cathedral began in 1512 under the leadership of Bishop Fray García Padilla, was continued from 1519 by Bishop Alexander Geraldini, and lasted until 1540. The cathedral's very first stone was laid in 1502 by Christopher Columbus' son Diego Columbus. The construction was carried out by Luis Moya, according to plans designed by Alonso Rodriguez, of Seville, Spain. It was consecrated in 1541.

The walls of the cathedral are solid limestone. There are twelve side chapels, three aisles, and a nave. None of the side chapels were included in the original building, but have been added on later. The cathedral is fronted with a golden-tinted coral limestone façade, the church combines elements of both Gothic and Baroque with some lavish plateresque styles as exemplified by the high altar chiseled out of silver. There is also a treasury which has an excellent art collection of ancient woodcarvings, furnishings, funerary monuments, silver, and jewelry.

The remains of Christopher Columbus were once housed at the cathedral, before their final resting place in the Faro a Colon.

Catedral de Santa María la Menor does not have a bell tower. Because of lacking funds, it took the Spanish 29 years to build, and some features had to be omitted due to lack of money. The biggest toll the cathedral took was when British pirate Sir Francis Drake captured it and used it as his fortress. The damage sustained by the cathedral during the Drake's attacks and subsequent looting and plundering left many of the artifacts and artwork damaged beyond recovery. As a matter of fact, the cathedral's most valued artwork - the Madonna from the Chapel of the Virgin of Antigua - was stolen and spirited off to Spain in 1520. It was not returned back to the Dominican Republic until 1892.
Codex

The Codex is here to help you distinguish fact from fiction. Everything in Conquistador is at least inspired either by historical events, people, and places, or by Native American mythology or Spanish legends. As you progress through the game, articles about the experiences you have in the game, and how they relate to actual history, will be gradually added to the Codex. If you ever find yourself wondering if something you just found in the game has any bearing in real life, check the Codex and see if it says anything about that subject.

Codex articles remain unlocked across subsequent playthroughs, so even if you start over on the game, your previously unlocked articles will remain unlocked.
El Dorado

The myth of the city of gold has its roots in legends told to the Spanish conquistadors about a tribe of natives high in the Andes mountains. According to these legends, the inauguration of their chiefs included a ceremony at the banks of the lake Guatavita. At this ceremony, the new chief was covered in gold dust, and an offering of gold and jewels was thrown into the depths of the lake to appease the god that lived underwater. Late in the 15th century, the tribe was conquered by another tribe and the custom of the ceremony by the lake ended.

The conquistadors called the golden chief "the gilded one" - El Dorado - and the legend evolved into a legend of a city made of gold. The Spaniards (and other Europeans) found the legend of the golden city easy to believe because they had found much gold among the natives. The golden city was never found, but the Spaniards did find lake Guatavita and tried to drain it. They succeeded in lowering the water table enough to obtain hundreds of pieces of gold and jewellery along the lakeshores, but they never found the rumoured treasure in the depths of the lake.
Fortaleza Ozama

Ozama is a Taino word that means wetlands or navigable waters. Fortaleza Ozama (Ozama Fortress) was built on the banks of the Ozama river, one of the most important rivers in the Dominican Republic. It springs in the North and runs 104 km (65 miles) until it reaches the Carribbean Ocean a few hundred meters from the Fortress.

The Fortaleza Ozama was constructed between 1502 and 1508 by order of the then Governor of Hispaniola, Fray Nicholas de Ovando, the founder of the city of Santo Domingo. It was built in order to defend the city against attacks by pirates and privateers. It has never been taken by force of arms.

One part of the Fortress is Torre del Homenaje or Tower of Homage. It was built in medieval style rising to a height of 18.5 meters (61 feet). It was built utilizing the labor of enslaved Tainos and Africans.

The tower is called Tower of Homage to glorify the Spanish conquistadors, who came there from Spain to conquer and colonise the newly discovered lands. It was from this fort in Old Santo Domingo that the famous expeditions of conquest began; Hernán Cortés in México, Diego Velásquez in Cuba, Francisco Pizarro in Perú, Alonso de Hojeda in Venezuela, Pazco Núñez Balboa in Panamá, and Ponce de León in Puerto Rico.

The tower was made of coral rock, which has the property of absorbing moisture, keeping the interior of the structure cool. No metals were used in the construction, and the cement - made of gypsum, clay, lime, and the blood of animals - becomes stronger with the passage of time.

Diego Colón, the son of Cristóbal Colón (Christopher Columbus) and his wife María de Toledo, temporarily lived in the Torre del Homenaje, occupying all of the second level, while their servants lived on the first level. The couple remained there for two years.
Fountain of Youth

The Fountain of Youth was first mentioned in the fifth century B.C. by the Greek historian Heroditus, who told about a fountain with a special kind of water in Ethiopia. The fountain crops up through history, both in connection to Alexander the great, in the legends of Al-Khidr, and others.

Through the ages, the tales of the fountain grew, and in the ages of exploration it was said that the land surrounding the fountain contained gold and riches, and that the fountain could make old men young again (presumably old women too).

Caribbean Indians told the European explorers of a land called "Bimini" somewhere to the north, where a fountain could restore old men to their youth and vitality.

Ponce de Leon is the person most commonly linked with the discovery of the Fountain of Youth. He was charged by the Spanish King to find, conquer, and colonise Bimini, and he set forth to look for it in 1513. It is believed that he was primarily looking for gold and slaves, and didn't give much credence to the legends of the fountain. He never mentioned finding the fountain, but because he landed in Florida, the fountain is now thought to be there.
Hispaniola

Hispaniola - formerly known as Española - is the second largest of the West Indian islands. Politically, it is divided into the republic of Haiti (West) and the Dominican Republic (East). Christopher Columbus landed on the island in 1492 and named it La Isla Espanola. As a Spanish colony the island was an excellent strategic location for the control of Spanish expansion to Cuba, Mexico, and Panama.

Columbus described the islands as a paradise. The natives - the Taino - he described as peaceful, generous, and cooperative. Because of that, the Spanish saw the island as a rich and easy target to conquer. The Spaniards forced the Taino into hard labour panning for gold under repressive working conditions.

During this period a great part of the original population on the island were killed by epidemics brought on by the Spanish conquerors. They were supplanted by African slaves, especially in the sugar plantations in the 16th century.
Masaya Volcano

The Masaya Volcanom, or the Masaya caldera, was formed 2500 years ago by a basaltic eruption of the Las Sierras shield volcano. The Masaya caldera covers 6 by 11.5 km and has all of 13 openings through which there is a constant emission of sulphur dioxide gas.

Masaya's last eruption of lava was in 1772. Since then, several minor explosions have occurred in addition to the emissions of gas.

The Masaya was feared both by the indigenous people and by the Spanish Conquistadors. It is told that the locals sought to appease the spirit of the volcano by sacrificing young girls, throwing them into the mouth of the volcano.

The Spanish Conquistadors at first thought the glistening lava was liquid gold, but as they experienced the heat and the poisonous fumes from the heart of the volcano, they named it "La Boca del Inferno" or "the Mouth of Hell". They also erected a cross on the edge of the crater and named it "La Cruz de Bobadilla" after Father Francisco Bobadilla, a Jesuit priest. By doing so, they hoped to exorcise the Devil.
Maya

The Maya lived in three loosely defined zones: The Maya highlands, the Southern lowlands, and the Northern lowlands (all of the Yucatán peninsula). The height of the Maya empire was around 600 A.D. Their cities spread through Mesoamerica, and varied greatly depending on the topography. They evolved as nature dictated, even in the tropical rainforests.

The Maya excelled at agriculture, pottery, hieroglyph writing, calendar-making and mathematics, and left behind an astonishing amount of impressive architecture and symbolic artwork such as the stepped pyramids, similar to the architecture of the Toltec.

Most of the great stone cities of the Maya were abandoned by 900 A.D., and by the time of the Spanish conquest, the Maya were primarily living in small farming communities. Development persisted in the northern centers and the cities of the northern lowlands in Yucatán continued to flourish for centuries more; some of the important sites in this era were Chichen Itza, Uxmal, Edzná, and Coba. After the decline of the ruling dynasties of Chichen and Uxmal, Mayapan ruled all of Yucatán until a revolt in 1450. After this point, the area degenerated into competing city-states until Yucatán was conquered by the Spanish.

The Spanish conquest of Yucatan lasted 170 years. Unlike the Aztec and Inca Empires, there was no single Maya political center, therefore the conquistadors had to subdue the numerous independent Maya states (polities) one by one, many of which fought fiercely.

The Maya survived the Spanish colonization. The Maya and their descendants form sizable populations throughout the Maya area and maintain a distinctive set of traditions and beliefs. Millions of people still speak Maya languages.
Moctezuma Xococytzin

Moctezuma II was also known as Motecuhzoma Xococytzin or Montezuma. The ninth emperor of the Aztecs, he was born around 1466 and became emperor in 1502. He ruled as emperor until 1520, when he was killed during a battle with the Spanish.

He inherited the throne from his uncle Ahuitzotl, who conquered vast areas and more than doubled the territory of Aztec dominance. Moctezuma served as a general in these battles of conquest, but during his reign he worked to consolidate the power over those newly conquered regions in preference to conquering new areas.

Moctezuma II received reports of strangers landing on the coast in 1517, and the 8th of November 1519 he met Cortés outside Tenochtitlan and welcomed the Spanish into his palace as guests. For unknown reasons, he was then imprisoned by the Spanish in his own home. Although Moctezuma II is traditionally believed to have been a harsh ruler, there is evidence that he was actually a good and clever ruler who has been misjudged on the background of his encounter with the Spanish and his subsequent capitulation.
Pearl Fishers of Cubaqua

The Venezuelan island Cubaqua was discovered in 1498 by Cristopher Columbus. At the time of Columbus' arrival in the new world, sources of gold, pearls and spices were a strong motivation for Spain to expand in the Americas. When Christopher Columbus brought samples of the riches of the Americas back to Spain, many expeditions were formed by explorers and adventurers to seek the riches of the newly discovered lands.

The first Spanish town in the new world was established in Cubaqua in 1528 to serve as a center for gathering pearls. The Spanish organised harvesting programs along the coasts of Venezuela and Colombia and shipped huge quantities of pearls to Europe. The north-east coast of Venezuela became known as "The Pearl Coast".

As a result of the intensive harvesting, the pearl oysters in Venezuela and Colombia had become much scarcer by the end of the 1500s, and as for the pearls of Cubaqua, which had been the island's greatest resource long before the arrival of the Europeans, the peak of its production of pearls was in the period 1508-1520. By the time of 1531, the results of overexploitation were evident.
San Tiago de los Caballeros

San Tiago de los Caballeros (Saint James of the Knights) also known as San Tiago de los 30 Caballeros, is the capital of Santiago Province. Whether founded in 1494 by Christopher Columbus (as some historians claim) or in 1495 by his brother Bartolomeo, San Tiago was among the first European settlements in America during the first wave of European colonization of the New World.

It is situated on the Yaque del Norte River, in the heart of the fertile Cibao Valley.

The original colony was in the city of Jacagua. In 1504, 30 caballeros of the Order of St. James (San Tiago) moved from nearby La Isabela to San Tiago,  and from that time the city was known as San Tiago de los Caballeros.

When the knights returned back to Spain they put a formal complaint before the king stating that their horses had been unfairly commissioned as beasts of burden and their weapons had been appropriated by Diego and Bartolome Columbus and that they had been made to do manual labor, something considered beneath their station as knights, who were meant to engage only in battle. The king compensated them for all their losses.

After being destroyed by an earthquake in 1562, the city was rebuilt a few miles away, where Nibaje Stream meets the Yaque; ruins of the old city are still visible in the district of San Francisco de Jacagua. San Tiago survived numerous earthquakes and fires to serve repeatedly as the republic's capital.
Santo Domingo

Santo Domingo is another name for the island Hispaniola, it was called so during the Spanish colonial times, and it has also been the name of the Eastern part of the island in recent times.

It was named after the major city on the Island, the city of Santo Domingo, founded by Christopher Columbus' brother, Bartholomew, in 1496, after the discovery of gold on the south coast of the island. He was at that time governor of the island, appointed by his brother Christopher.

The gold deposits of Hispaniola were just about depleted in 1515 and shortly after that, Hernando Cortes conquered Mexico and the fabulous riches of silver there attracted the Spaniards already residing in Santo Domingo. The island was abandoned and only a few thousand settlers remained, many of them of mixed Spanish/native heritage, making a living by raising livestock to supply the Spanish ships passing by on their way to the richer colonies on the American mainland.
Spanish Conquistadors

The conquistadors were the soldiers and explorers who conquered most of North and South America and put it under Spanish rule in the 15th, 16th, and 17th centuries.

Most of them were of noble descent and had already served as soldiers in Spanish battles in Europe. They were mostly volunteers in the Americas, providing their own weapons and materials. The captains were appointed by the Spanish crown, and were accorded authority under royal commission.

The first encounter between the conquistadors and the American natives ended with many of the Spaniards being taken as slaves by the Mayans. But that was the first time. The next expedition, better equipped and with great horses, turned the tables on the Mayans. The horses astounded the natives, and it is reported that a handful of Spanish riders were able to keep 10,000 warriors in check.

The conquistadors often overstepped the authority they had been accorded, most notably Hernán Cortés, who ordered all of his expedition's ships burned, and founded a city on the mainland. They were often ruthless in their quest for wealth and power, and were accused of cruelty and barbary by some of their more humane contemporaries.
Taíno

The Taíno Indian are a subgroup of the Arawakan Indians, who are thought to have originated in South America before migrating to the Caribbean. When Christopher Columbus arrived to the New World, Taíno Indians inhabited the Greater Antilles (Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola, Haiti, and Puerto Rico) in the Caribbean Sea. According to their own myths, the Taíno Indians were created in a cave on Hispaniola.

Taíno society on Hispaniola is believed to have developed between 1100 and 1500 AD. By the time of Columbus's arrival, their society was comprised of about 20 political chiefdoms, each one ruled by a cacique (chief). It is estimated that there were between 30,000 and 50,000 Taínos on Hispaniola when the Spanish arrived.

The Taínos were skilled at agriculture and hunting.  They were also good sailors, fishermen, canoe makers, and navigators. They had no calendar or writing system, and could only count to twenty, using their hands and feet.

The Spaniards expected the Taíno Indians to acknowledge the sovereignty of the king of Spain by payment of gold tribute, to work and supply provisions of food, and to observe Christian ways. The Taínos rebelled most notably in 1511, when several caciques conspired to oust the Spaniards. They were joined in this uprising by their traditional enemies, the Caribs. Their weapons, however, were no match against Spanish horses and firearms and the revolt was soon ended brutally by the Spanish forces of Governor Juan Ponce de León.

By 1514, there were fewer than 4000 Taínos left, and in 1519 a smallpox epidemic is said to have virtually wiped out the rest of the remaining population.
Tenochtitlan

Tenochtitlan was the Aztec capital at the time of the Spanish conquest in 1521, and was one of the largest cities in the world with perhaps as many as 200,000 inhabitants. The city was laid out in a grid divided by a network of streets and canals and was linked to the cities on the shores of the lake by raised causeways. It has been described as a beautiful and impressive city, with huge blue and red pyramids and white palaces.

Tenochtitlan was the political, economic, and religious center of the greatest empire of Precolumbian Mexico, and its great wealth was obtained not only from trade and industry, but also in great part from the spoils and tributes from the regions conquered by the Aztecs.

The Sacred Precinct with room for more than 8000 people was the heart of Tenochtitlan. It was the religious and ceremonial center of both the city and the empire, the most important Aztec gods had their temples there, and there were schools for training of young noblemen for the priesthood, priests' quarters, and ballcourts.

Adjacent to the Sacred Precinct was the royal palace, the homes of the nobles, and the administrative buildings. This area also featured beautiful gardens, zoos, and aviaries.

The common people lived at a distance in neighbourhoods with their own local temples and markets.
Tlaxcala

In the middle of the 14th century, the Tlaxcalteca defeated the Teo-Chichimeca and founded a small but powerful empire in the region that now bears their name. They were skilled fighters who followed the god of war and hunting, Camaxtli.

Owing to their military prowess, Tlaxcala was one of the few areas that the Aztecs couldn't subjugate, but the Aztec conquest of the surrounding area cut off Tlaxcala’s commerce. This situation was maintained until the arrival of the Spanish in the early 16th century.

One of the first major cities encountered by the Spanish on their way into Mexico was Tlaxcala. Cortés tried to negotiate a truce so the Spanish army could pass through Tlaxcala, but the Tlaxcalteca didn't understand the Spanish letters brought by envoys from Cempoala, and assumed that the Spaniards and their new Cempoalan allies had come to attack them.

After several battles and raids, resulting in great losses on both sides, the Tlaxcalteca agreed to assist the Spanish rather than having their houses destroyed and their women and children killed. The Tlaxcalteca explained to Cortés that they and the Mexica were old adversaries whose quarrel dated back many years. Cortés used this dispute to his advantage, and convinced the Tlaxcalteca to assist him on his march to Tenochtitlan. In exchange for their support, he promised not to levy taxes on them or confiscate their land.

In 1521 the alliance succeeded, firmly establishing Spanish control of central Mexico.  Afterward, the Tlaxcalteca continued to aid the Spaniards, fighting against other indigenous tribes and settling the newly conquered territories.
Toltec

In the 9th and 10th centuries, several groups of migrants came from the North and South to the Mesoamerican plains/The Mexican Basin. One of the first groups was the Toltecs, supposed to be escapees from the fall of Teotihuacán. The Toltecs founded the city of Tula or Tollan, which became the dominant city in Mesoamerica 900-1100, although it never reached the same size as Teotihuacán due to competing cities in the area.

The Toltec culture disappeared in the 12th century, possibly overrun by the Chichimecas. The Chichimecas' culture slowly disappeared, and central Mexico entered a chaotic dark age until the Aztecs rose to power in Tenochtitlán at what is now Mexico City, in the early 1300s.

The Aztecs respected the Toltecs as "men of knowledge", and rewrote some of their own history to show they were related to the Toltecs. The word Toltec is said to come from the Nahuatl language of that area, and means "master builder" or "artist".
 
There are no written records left by the Toltec. What we know about them is what we see in the ruins they left behind, and what later Mesoamerican people have written. We don't know what language they spoke, but it is supposed to have been some form of Nahuatl.

We also don't know whether the Toltec civilization was an empire in its own right (some call it the third of the great empires in the Basin of Mexico) or whether it was a mythical and philosophical construct by the Aztecs or other Mesoamericans that was used to symbolize the might and sophistication of several different civilizations. However, traces of their culture can be found even among the Mayans in Chichén Itza, 1500 km from Tula and in the Northamerican Southwest.
Totonac

The Totonac people resided in the eastern coastal and mountainous regions of Mexico at the time of the Spanish arrival in 1519. They are one of the possible builders of the Pre-Columbian city of El Tajín, and further maintained quarters in Teotihuacán (a city which they claim to have built). Until the mid-19th century they were the world's main producers of vanilla.

The Aztecs labeled the region of the Totonac "Totonacapan"; which then extended roughly from Papantla in the north to Cempoala in the south. Totonacapan was largely hot and humid. Along with the normal agricultural crops of maize, manioc, squash, beans, pumpkin, and chili peppers, the region was noted for its production of liquid amber and cotton. Even during the disastrous central Mexican famine of 1450-1454, the region remained fertile and many Aztecs were forced to sell themselves or their family members as slaves to the Totonac in exchange for subsistence maize.

The region of Totonacapan was subject to Aztec military incursions from the mid-15th century until the Spanish arrival. The Aztec built fortifications throughout the region, but there were several rebellions against their rule.

Major Totonac centers were Papantla, with an estimated population of 60,000 in 1519, Xalapa (around 120,000), and Cempoala (around 80,000). Cempoala was the first indigenous city state visited by Hernán Cortés in his march to the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlán. The Totonacs of Cempoala joined forces with Cortés and, along with the Tlaxcalan Indians, contributed significantly to the Spanish conquest.
Xipe Totec

The name Xipe Totec means "Our Lord the Flayed One", and he was usually depicted as a flayed man clad in his own skin.

He was the Aztec god of agriculture, spring, and seasons, and the symbol of the death and rebirth of nature. Xipe Totec was also the god of the east and the patron of gold smiths.

He was called the flayed god, because according to myth, he flayed himself to stimulate growth in both nature and man. When he had shed his skin, he would reappear as a shining, golden god.

Each year in the beginning of spring, he was honoured by human sacrifices. The priests removed the hearts from the victims while they were still alive, then the priests flayed the bodies and put on the skins, which had been coloured yellow. The yellow skins were called teocuitlaquemitl (golden clothes). Other victims were fastened to a frame and killed with arrows. The blood dripping from these sacrifizes symbolised the fertile spring rain. These rituals symbolized the renewal of the earth and the budding of new life.

Xipe Totec was also known by the names Tlatlauhca, Tlatlauhqui Tezcatlipoca ("Red Smoking Mirror") and Youalahuan ("the Night Drinker").
Xolotl

Xolotl was known as The Twin or The Lord of the West, and was the god of fire and bad luck. He was Quetzalcoatl's twin, sons of the virgin Coatlicue, and Quetzalcoatl's double. He was the dark personification of Venus, the evening star, and he guarded the sun on its journey through the underworld at night.

He was a dog-like deity, often depicted with ragged ears, and was identified with sickness and physical deformity. He was also sometimes depicted as a skeleton or a man with the head of a dog (dogs were considered filthy and immoral in the Mesoamerican cultures, and likewise, twins were considered a type of deformity).

According to myth, he accompanied Quetzalcoatl to Mictlan, the land of death, to retrieve the bones from those who inhabited the previous world (Nahui Atl) in order to create new life for this world (Nahui Olin), and he assisted Quetzalcoatl in bringing humankind and fire from the underworld.

In another creation myth it was Xolotl who brought a bone to the gods, who sprinkled it with some of their blood and transformed it into a boy and a girl: the first of the human race.
